facts.text: Find the treasure shown on the party's treasure map.
Where are the locations marked on the treasure map, and which of them holds the treasure?

classification.grounding_justification: The map's marked locations are an established, unresolved feature of the party's map.
classification.investigative_depth_justification: Locating the marks and finding which holds treasure is mostly a matter of exploration rather than uncovering a hidden situation.
classification.narrative_payoff_justification: Finding the treasure site would be useful and somewhat satisfying but mainly instrumental.
classification.investigative_potential_justification: Checking marked sites in the field supports following leads across several locations.

facts.text: One location marked on the treasure map lies along the party's route north to the Barrow, and the party means to check it on the way.

classification.support_basis: Checking a marked site could reveal the treasure or rule out one location, though nothing establishes this site holds it.

facts.text: Reginald the Frog warns that a little trickster called a Clurichen comes from the riverbanks into Brandonsford every night, up to no good, and that the party should stay away from wherever it goes.
facts.ended_how: no longer relevant: the Clurichen, Naggeneen, was caught and now hangs captive in a bag behind Quinn's bar

classification.negative_outcome_clarity_justification: Reginald only said the creature was up to no good, with no specific harm named.
classification.outcome_severity_justification: No harm beyond vague mischief was established; it turned out to be booze theft.
classification.evidentiary_strength_justification: Rested on Reginald's warning; the creature's nightly visits were confirmed.
classification.evidence_of_progression_justification: Nightly visits were a pattern, but no escalating harm was shown.
classification.preventability_justification: The party could avoid it or catch it, as they did.

facts.text: What is the Clurichen doing when it comes into Brandonsford from the riverbanks each night?
facts.ended_how: answered: Naggeneen sneaks invisibly into the Golden Egg's basement to steal and drink Quinn's alcohol

classification.grounding_justification: Reginald's warning about nightly visits clearly raised the question.
classification.investigative_depth_justification: Answering it revealed a hidden activity behind Quinn's missing booze.
classification.narrative_payoff_justification: The answer explained the booze thefts, mildly interesting.
classification.investigative_potential_justification: It supported following footprints and staking out the river.

facts.text: Naggeneen the Clurichen, hanging captive in a bag behind Quinn's bar, offers his pot of gold or a secret to whoever lets him go; Sir Phidipaldi refused and handed him to Quinn.

classification.support_basis: Play ties neither the gold nor the secret to any want or debt of the party, and freeing him now means going behind Quinn's back.

facts.text: What does Quinn intend to do with the captive Naggeneen?

classification.grounding_justification: Quinn pointedly said he knew what he would do with this one without saying what, and the bag still hangs behind his bar.
classification.investigative_depth_justification: It reveals one man's intention; a single conversation would likely settle it.
classification.narrative_payoff_justification: Mildly interesting fate of a minor creature.
classification.investigative_potential_justification: Little beyond asking Quinn or watching the bar.

facts.text: Kill the black dragon near Brandonsford and drag its body into town to collect Eric the Reeve's 1000 gold bounty.
George, a capable woodsman living a couple of houses from the Clumsy Fox who lost an arm to the dragon, could tell the party about his encounter; Eric says he might show up at the tavern tonight.
facts.ended_how: used up: Sir Phidipaldi visited George and heard his account

classification.support_basis: George's firsthand account would inform the party about the dragon before they hunt it.

facts.text: Lady Hilda offers to join the party for pay on the dragon hunt.
facts.ended_how: no longer relevant here: the offer is held on its own thread, thread_4

classification.support_basis: An extra hired fighter would add strength to the hunt.

facts.text: Where did this black dragon come from, when Sir Brandon's dragon was killed and torn apart centuries ago?

classification.grounding_justification: The legend says Brandon's dragon died long ago, yet a black dragon is active now, a clear contradiction.
classification.investigative_depth_justification: The answer would reveal the dragon's origin and its link to the old legend.
classification.narrative_payoff_justification: Learning whether it is the same dragon or a new one would reshape understanding of the legend.
classification.investigative_potential_justification: Legends, Gill's fairytales and the Barrow offer leads.

facts.text: George says the black dragon cannot fly yet but soon will, and then the town is doomed; it already tore off George's arm and killed his friends, and Gill's three sons are out hunting it.

classification.negative_outcome_clarity_justification: A flying dragon dooming the town, and deaths of hunters, are specific outcomes.
classification.outcome_severity_justification: The town's doom and deaths of hunters affect many.
classification.evidentiary_strength_justification: George is an eyewitness survivor, though his forecast about flight is his own.
classification.evidence_of_progression_justification: The dragon is described as about to gain flight, an advancing process, and has already killed.
classification.preventability_justification: Killing it may require Brandon's sword, which the party is pursuing, but means are uncertain.

facts.text: George says the dragon's lair is up north at the foot of the mountains, reachable without climbing.

classification.support_basis: Knowing where the lair is lets the party find the dragon to kill it.

facts.text: George says nothing pierces the dragon's black scales, as all their arrows and swords failed; its poisonous bite kills and it spits sulfur.
Father William says the dragon cannot be killed without Brandon's sword from the Barrow Mound (see thread_12).

classification.support_basis: The sword is reportedly the only way past the dragon's invulnerability, though this rests on legend and Father William's word.

facts.text: Dunk says Warwick's shimmering armor could help against the dragon (see thread_8).

classification.support_basis: Magical armor would reduce the risk of the dragon's attacks, though the party does not have it yet.

facts.text: Does Eric the Reeve actually have the 1000 gold he promised for killing the dragon?

classification.grounding_justification: George explicitly voices doubt that Eric has the money.
classification.investigative_depth_justification: A single check on Eric's finances would settle it.
classification.narrative_payoff_justification: Mainly practical, though it could expose Eric as dishonest.
classification.investigative_potential_justification: Little beyond questioning Eric or checking his coffers.

facts.text: George allows that Sir Phidipaldi's lance may be one of the few weapons not yet tried against the dragon.

classification.support_basis: An untried weapon offers a slim chance against scales nothing else pierced, with no evidence it works.

facts.text: Sir Phidipaldi vowed to George to bring his lance against the dragon.

classification.stake_basis: George merely remarked the lance might be untried; no reliance by George on this performance is established.

facts.text: Lady Hilda, a seasoned-looking noblewoman with chain mail and a shield, offers to join the party for money for the dragon hunt; she says she cannot kill the dragon herself, and no fee has been named.

classification.support_basis: An armored, experienced fighter would add strength to the dragon hunt, though she admits she cannot kill the dragon herself and her fee is unknown.

facts.text: Sir Phidipaldi told Lady Hilda the party would talk with Eric the Reeve and come back to her to take up her services.

classification.stake_basis: Lady Hilda wants paid work on the dragon hunt and was told the party would return to hire her, but no reliance beyond a modest interest in the job is established.

facts.text: Drop Dead Ned, a thief with a killer wasp in a jar on his necklace, offers himself and the wasp for hire at 100 gold a week, as long as he gets to kill people with the wasp. For a night of at least ten kills, he would give back 5 gold per kill if he can do what he wants with the bodies. Dr. Uriah said he would think about it.

classification.support_basis: Ned is still at the Clumsy Fox adventurers' table (beat_6), but play has tied his hire to no specific want or debt of the party; his terms require letting him kill people, which limits his use.

facts.text: What happened to Brandonsford's restocking shipment, due a week ago, and why have no goods reached town in months?

classification.grounding_justification: The fiction notes again that shipments to Brandonsford still have not come in, keeping the prolonged absence of goods conspicuous.
classification.investigative_depth_justification: The answer would reveal a hidden cause behind months of missing deliveries, an underlying circumstance rather than a simple fact.
classification.narrative_payoff_justification: Explaining why a whole town has been cut off would change the party's understanding of the region's troubles.
classification.investigative_potential_justification: Tracing a missing shipment along its route and questioning townsfolk plausibly supports following leads.

facts.text: Dunk is weighing acquiring Farmer Gill's shabby prize mule, Shamus, which Gill suggests would let him start his own farm.

Farmer Gill offers to sell Shamus to Dunk for 100 gold; he turned down Dunk's 20 gold offer but says he will lower the price once his boys come back, since without them or the mule he can't get work done.

classification.support_basis: Buying Shamus is the established way to get the mule, though the current price is high and a lower price depends on Gill's sons returning.

facts.text: When Dunk asked to trade work for Shamus, Gill said the big work needed was killing the dragon outside town; no deal was agreed.

classification.support_basis: Gill only hinted that killing the dragon is the work he needs; no trade of the mule for that work was agreed, so it is doubtful as a route to Shamus.

facts.text: Warwick the smith displays a mithril chain shirt in his shop that Dunk saw glowing in the moonlight and is clearly magical; Dunk says it could help against the dragon and plans to get it. Gill says it would fit a normal-sized person but not Dunk, and that Warwick always refuses to sell it.

classification.support_basis: Magical mithril armor would protect a party member fighting a dragon with deadly poison bites and sulfur spit, though Warwick won't sell it, it won't fit Dunk, and its exact magic is unknown.

facts.text: Why is Warwick growing more paranoid and covering his shop in lucky charms and clovers? Gill thinks it is to keep away Ingrid the potion seller, who fancies him.
facts.ended_how: answered: Ingrid climbs up every night to leave gifts on Warwick's windowsill and watch him sleep, which largely explains his paranoia

classification.grounding_justification: Gill described Warwick's growing paranoia and the charms covering his shop, a visible anomaly.
classification.investigative_depth_justification: The answer revealed a hidden circumstance: Ingrid's secret nightly visits.
classification.narrative_payoff_justification: The secret of Ingrid's nightly watching is a mildly surprising revelation.
classification.investigative_potential_justification: Questioning Ingrid or Warwick was enough to answer it.

facts.text: Sir Phidipaldi agreed to help Quinn get back at Bentley, whom Quinn blames for stealing his ale at night; Quinn promised him 100 gold for that help.
facts.ended_how: fulfilled: the party caught the real thief in Quinn's basement and Quinn paid Sir Phidipaldi, Trout and Dr. Uriah 33 gold each (beat_22)

classification.stake_basis: Quinn was losing his stock every night and wanted the thief stopped, paying for the help.

facts.text: Sir Phidipaldi agreed to stage a fake ale delivery at the Golden Egg: Quinn brings up bottles, they fill them with water, and Sir Phidipaldi makes a big show of coming in to deliver them, to see what happens.
facts.ended_how: obsolete: the thief was caught in the basement without the staged delivery, and Quinn paid for the help (beat_21, beat_22)

classification.stake_basis: The staged delivery was only a shared plan to see what happens; Quinn's interest was in catching the thief, not in this performance.

facts.text: What empties or knocks over Quinn's stock every night at the Golden Egg? Quinn blames Bentley.
facts.ended_how: answered: the Clurichen Naggeneen, not Bentley, was taking Quinn's alcohol (beat_21)

classification.grounding_justification: Quinn's nightly losses were conspicuous and framed as an unexplained theft he blamed on Bentley.
classification.investigative_depth_justification: The answer revealed a hidden culprit behind repeated nightly losses, contradicting Quinn's suspicion.
classification.narrative_payoff_justification: Revealing an invisible Clurichen instead of Bentley changed the understanding of events.
classification.investigative_potential_justification: It supported a stakeout, tracking footprints and trapping the thief.

facts.text: Under Trout's Halfling Corps terms, Squints gets second pick of the party's first treasure, after the elite members pick, in return for funding himself and his gear until then and taking Trout's orders.

classification.stake_basis: Squints is funding himself and fighting monsters for nothing until the first treasure, relying on this pick as his only pay.

facts.text: Squints, a halfling with sling and dagger and a more experienced fighter than Trout, follows Trout's orders as junior assistant in the Halfling Corps.

classification.support_basis: An extra capable fighter and scout who will take on risky tasks, though play ties him to no specific want or debt.

facts.text: Trout told Brother Dirk he reports to Squints, who is pleased to have a follower; Dirk had said he should just head home.
facts.uncertain_reason: Play never shows Dirk accepting the arrangement, and he had said he would head home.

classification.support_basis: Adds Dirk as a follower under Squints, but play ties this to no want or debt and Dirk's agreement is unclear.

facts.text: Trout sends Squints into danger while privately telling the party they will not rescue him if he is caught, so Squints may be left to die on one of Trout's orders.

classification.negative_outcome_clarity_justification: The harm is Squints being abandoned when caught on a dangerous errand.
classification.outcome_severity_justification: Death or serious harm to one ally.
classification.evidentiary_strength_justification: Trout said so directly and Phidipaldi agreed.
classification.evidence_of_progression_justification: Trout already sent him alone past a giant and hit him with a sling, but no further mission is set.
classification.preventability_justification: The party controls whether it orders Squints into danger and whether it rescues him.

facts.text: Ingrid is brewing a sleeping potion from the faun wine Dunk gave her. Dunk plans to use it to keep Warwick asleep while he gets into the house. He is due to collect it tonight.

classification.support_basis: A sleeping Warwick would let Dunk enter the house and reach the mithril shirt unopposed. It is doubtful whether the potion will work, because the faun wine was heavily diluted and Father William claims Ingrid cannot make her potions herself.

facts.text: In exchange for Ingrid making the sleeping potion, Dunk is to meet her tonight and help her get into Warwick's house and dose him, so she can watch Warwick all night without fear of waking him.

classification.stake_basis: Ingrid is making the potion specifically so she can watch Warwick without fear of him waking, and she relies on Dunk to get her in and administer it.

facts.text: Dunk knows Ingrid's secret love for Warwick. Her greatest fear is that Warwick learns she watches him through his window, and Dunk has hinted he hasn't kept the secret yet. This gives him leverage over her.

classification.support_basis: The threat of exposure could pressure Ingrid into cooperating, for example by unlocking Warwick's door. So far she has balked at crawling into the house.

facts.text: Warwick sleeps in a second-story bedroom whose window is left cracked open. Ingrid climbs up to it every night.

classification.support_basis: The open window is a known, climbable way into Warwick's house, where the mithril shirt is kept.

facts.text: Can Ingrid make a working sleeping potion from the heavily diluted faun wine?

classification.grounding_justification: Dunk deliberately diluted the key ingredient to 20%, and Father William claims Ingrid cannot make her own potions, which she disputes. Together these clearly raise the question.
classification.investigative_depth_justification: The answer settles a property of one potion, plus a little about Ingrid's skill.
classification.narrative_payoff_justification: The answer is mainly instrumental to the scheme, with mild interest in whether Ingrid is a fraud.
classification.investigative_potential_justification: It will be settled by collecting and using the potion.

facts.text: The fauns at the Faun Grove, north of town across the river, trade their sleep-inducing wine for sentimental items such as a love letter or a pixie's treasure.

classification.support_basis: The fauns are a source of more undiluted wine if the potion fails or more is needed, at the cost of a sentimental trade item.

facts.text: Father William says the dragon cannot be killed without the magic sword buried with Brandon in the Barrow Mound; the party is walking to the Barrow to get it.

classification.support_basis: George says nothing pierces the dragon's scales, and Father William says only this sword can kill it, though George says no one knows what is true of the legend or where the sword is.

facts.text: Father William marked the Barrow Mound on Dr. Uriah's map; the party reckons it a three-mile walk through the forest, though Father William called it about a day's walk.

classification.support_basis: The marked map lets the party find the Barrow where the sword is said to lie; the distance is disputed.

facts.text: What is the truth of the legend of Brandon's fairy-given sword, and is it really in the Barrow Mound?

classification.grounding_justification: George explicitly says no one knows what is true of the legend or where the sword is, while Father William says it is buried with Brandon.
classification.investigative_depth_justification: The answer would reveal the real history behind Brandon's killing of the dragon and the sword's nature.
classification.narrative_payoff_justification: Confirming or overturning a centuries-old legend would change the party's understanding of how the dragon can be beaten.
classification.investigative_potential_justification: Farmer Gill knows the fairytales, and the Barrow itself can be explored.

facts.text: George says Farmer Gill knows the fairytales about Sir Brandon and his fairy-given sword.

classification.support_basis: Asking Gill could clarify the legend of the sword the party seeks to kill the dragon, though fairytales may be unreliable.

facts.text: Dr. Uriah owes Father William penance at the Barrow Mound, agreed in exchange for William marking the Barrow Mound and the witch's home on his map.

classification.stake_basis: Father William set the penance as his price for marking the map, reflecting his religious concern about the Dagonite Uriah, but no further reliance on it is shown.

facts.text: Dr. Uriah owes Father William a 10 gold donation for upkeep, agreed in exchange for William marking the map.

classification.stake_basis: Father William asked for the 10 gold specifically for upkeep as payment for marking the map; a modest concrete interest.

facts.text: A man-eating giant lives in an oversized stone cottage in a clearing in the woods north of town, on the party's route north; Brother Dirk says the giant captured him and meant to eat him in a stew. The giant is unharmed, and the party has just robbed him and broken his window.

classification.negative_outcome_clarity_justification: The specific harm is clear: the giant captures travellers and cooks and eats them.
classification.outcome_severity_justification: Being captured and eaten means death.
classification.evidentiary_strength_justification: The party saw Dirk bound in a sack beside the cooking pot and the giant chasing them, and Dirk testified that the giant meant to eat him.
classification.evidence_of_progression_justification: The giant is still active at his cottage on the route north and has already caught one traveller. There is no established sign that he is hunting the party now.
classification.preventability_justification: The party knows where the cottage is, can route around it, and has shown that the slow giant is easily outrun.
